Hi all.  John has raised some intriguing issues in his post and has  
generated quite a bit of off-list email traffic among the statnet  
team.  To summarize briefly:


Point (3) appears to refer to the fact, alluded to by Michal and  
Magnus and Pavel already, that the latentnet package (in statnet) has  
to date depended on the mclust package (not written by us and not in  
statnet).  This dependency is going away, and in fact Pavel reports  
that a new version of latentnet is already percolating through CRAN.   
Otherwise, all statnet code is, and has always been, GPL; details are  
at http://statnetproject.org/attribution


Point (2) is trickier to parse.  There are undoubtedly some issues of  
legacy code (parts of sna are over 10 years old, after all!) but the  
fact is that there is no way to make statnet packages do what they do,  
as fast as they do it, by writing in R only. Multiple cores do not  
change this fact.  That said, statnet does rely on R for a lot of its  
heavy lifting when possible.  Nothing about the statnet packages is  
unusual, relative to many other R packages, in these regards.


As for (1), it is important to keep in mind that ergms are not glms.   
The "unusual modification" is not a creation of statnet; it is the  
reality of these models.  Thus, there is no way to use completely  
standard glm syntax in formulating an ergm specification; the choice  
is between creating a completely new syntax and bending the existing  
formula structure.  We are still convinced that the latter is by far  
the better choice in terms of consistency with the R paradigm.  (We  
thought very carefully about this issue when the ergm package was in  
its infancy!)

Note that in some cases, an ergm coincides with a logistic regression  
model, which *is* a glm.  In such cases, one could in fact use a more  
traditional glm-like syntax, but even in these cases, the bookkeeping  
necessary to create the traditional predictor matrix is pretty  
complicated and would require its own brand-new syntax since we would  
certainly want to create methods to help the user do this.  Our choice  
of ergm syntax is thus a massive benefit to simplicity.

There is quite a bit more room for discussion of this question, and  
undoubtedly if others have questions/suggestions then this could  
create some more lively discussion on this list.  In particular, if  
novice (or not-so-novice) users are confused about the similarities  
and differences between an ergm, with its inherent auto-dependency,  
and a glm, please ask!  It's a great topic for this list.


Finally, kudos to Michal for what sounds like great work on the  
intergraph package!  I won't address the namespace issue, the only  
real way in which statnet currently doesn't "play well" in my opinion,  
except to say that Michal and Magnus offer very persuasive arguments  
in favor of namespaces and we will probably add them in future statnet  
releases (as others have stated or surmised, namespaces did not exist  
in their current form when we began statnet).



Thanks to all for keeping discussions professional and respectful.

Dave
for the statnet team:  Mark, Carter, Steve, Martina, Pavel




On Aug 30, 2010, at 8:43 AM, John Paolillo wrote:

> The point about namespaces is well-made by Michal, but really it  
> should have been obvious and best practice would have indicated  
> using R namespaces at the outset of the Statnet project.  
> Unfortunately, this is just one of the programming practices that  
> the Statnet project has adopted that runs counter to the R  
> environment that they chose to work within. To the namespace issue  
> may be added at least the following three:
>
> (1) Statnet imposes an unusual modification on the semantics of  
> formula objects in R. In no other R package does one write a formula  
> in which complex object (i.e. the network, which contains many  
> vectors of differing lengths) is expressed in terms of objects  
> contained within it.
>
> (2) Insistence on C code (ostensibly for speed), to the point of  
> incorporating legacy code that duplicates basic functionality of the  
> BLAS in R (e.g. eigen decomposition). This actually flies in the  
> face of the speed criterion, because the R BLAS is optimized for  
> multiple-core architectures (not as common when the Statnet project  
> started as they are now), and the legacy code is not (nor is  
> specialized Statnet C code like the network layout code necessarily  
> multi-processor optimized).
>
> (3) Statnet has dependencies on packages that bear a UW license  
> which is NOT compatible with GPL licenses, meaning that Statnet and  
> code that uses Statnet packages raise legal complications regarding  
> licensing that are likely to surprise many users. Specifically, "for  
> profit" uses of some parts of the code potentially require payment  
> of royalty fees to UW (the GPL license of R has no such restriction).
>
> The above problems, like the namespace issue, make Statnet not play  
> well with other packages, and for this reason any use of Statnet is  
> awkward for me. It would be good if the Statnet team could give some  
> attention to them, so that it can interoperate better with R and  
> other R packages.
>
> John Paolillo

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Martin -

Your performance will depend on how dense your network is, how much 
memory you have, etc.  If you are seeing low CPU utilization, you 
probably have a memory issue.  Using the leanest available 
representations can help (e.g., sna edgelists if you don't need 
metadata), but very large graphs (like other large things) are expensive.

In like vein, you will find that certain calculations are intrinsically 
costly for large graphs (unless they are _extremely_ sparse, and 
sometimes even then).  Things like betweenness/closeness calculation, 
clique enumeration, and cycle enumeration, geodesics, etc. are not 
cheap,* however classic they may be.  (kcores and degree are examples of 
cheap computations, however, and if those are running slow then you 
should check your memory utilization.)

If performance is an issue, you might ask yourself why you are trying to 
calculate something like betweenness on this large graph, and whether 
you actually need the entire structure to answer your question. 
Whenever one deals with very large data sets (as is common in fields 
such as, say, GIS), it pays to think about efficiency when approaching 
one's research problem.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

*Although fast _approximate_ algorithms are sometimes available for 
these quantities.  This is an area of active research.

Martin Klaus wrote:
> Dear Carter,

> measures and e.g. degee ist easy and on that way very fast. But I 
> expected my new PC, which by the way has 24 GB of memory, should be fast 
> than e.g a java compiled program like ORA. But ORA was 5 times faster 
> than R and it used the full 99.9% of the CPU for the whole time of 
> calculation. That is why I thought it would be possible to tell R to use 
> more of the possible CPU AND memory ;)
> But the way I understand you it is not possible to adjust theses things 
> in the statnet packge or in R at any other point?!
> Thanks again for your help,

OK, from what has been said, it sounds like your issue may be that you 
are looking at _total_ CPU utilization, not utilization of a specific 
CPU.  Parallel processing is gradually coming into play within R, and 
you can employ it at user-level via libraries like snow and multicore. 
For the most part, however, R is still engineered around a 
single-processor environment.  The simplest way to exploit 
multi-processor capabilities for a problem like yours would be to use a 
package like multicore, and set your various analysis tasks running in 
parallel.  Even if each task is serially executed, the set of tasks will 
be completed more quickly.  (That's one of the tactics I sometimes use. 
  In fact, there are advantages of this strategy in a clustered 
environment, because it's easier to control how many processors I'm 
eating (and how much the other users will resent my presence).)  As 
parallel processing support stabilizes, I think you'll see it used more 
extensively within R generally (and in statnet -- see the help for 
control.ergm for one currently implemented example).

As far as ORA, my understanding is that the important parts are all 
written in C++ (unless they have rewritten it since, which is always 
possible).  (Fun bit of trivia: when I was in Kathleen's lab at CMU, I 
wrote a collection of C routines called "netstat" that ultimately became 
part of the first ORA backend.  All of that code was rewritten long ago, 
of course, and I doubt that ORA today retains any influence from the old 
netstat base.)  If the CMU folks have done their homework (and they 
usually do), ORA _should_ outperform R-based tools on many tasks, since 
it's a custom-built piece of compiled code, while R libraries have large 
chunks of comparatively slow interpreted code.  That's the price you pay 
for ease of use, flexibility, ability to interoperate with other 
libraries, etc.  I'd guess that much of that factor of 5 is a multiple 
core issue, but even so I would not be surprised to find that many tasks 
run somewhat faster in ORA (or any dedicated, standalone application) 
than in R/statnet.  If they didn't, the number of situations in which 
such standalone tools would be at all preferable to general-purpose 
platforms like R would be very circumscribed.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi, folks -

Here is a four-part answer to this question:

1. If your goal is to test for marginal (non)association between an NLI 
(e.g., closeness) and a node-level covariate, IMHO the most 
straightforward approach is to use permutation procedures.  If you want 
a quick tutorial, you might check out the associated portion of the 
statnet workshop we gave at this year's Political Networks meeting; the 
URL is 
http://lectopia.oit.duke.edu/ilectures/ilectures.lasso?ut=1065&id=27647, 
and the discussion starts at around 48 minutes.  (Part 1 of the day's 
session is at 
http://lectopia.oit.duke.edu/ilectures/ilectures.lasso?ut=1065&id=27647, 
for those who are interested.)   As I note in response to a question 
from the audience, generalizing this to the multivariate case is 
possible, but one runs into complications that make the approach less 
attractive.  For the simple, bivariate case, however, my sense is that 
permutation tests are often a good starting point.

2. For more complex, parametric versions of the covariate/NLI question, 
the natural approach is to construct a statistic based on an interaction 
of the covariate with the NLI, and employ an ERG model.  (This is 
equivalent to what nodecov does, with the NLI here being degree.)  We 
have talked for years about adding equivalent terms for other centrality 
scores, but I am not sure if anything is implemented at present -- there 
are no special theoretical issues, but the computation can be painful. 
(I regularly hassle my CS colleagues for the algorithmic developments we 
need to make changescore calculation fast for indices like betweenness, 
but am assured that this is a non-trivial research problem.  :-))  I 
spoke with Mark about putting something crude together a few months ago, 
but am not sure if he's had time to make progress on it -- it's clear 
that this would be a very interesting set of terms to be able to 
include.  Having said that, we don't know how stable models built from 
those terms would be, so this might turn out to be harder in practice 
than it seems.

3. A fact little remembered today is that the ERG were introduced in 
part to act as non-trivial null models against which to test for complex 
structural biases.  (See the discussion in Holland and Leinhardt, JASA, 
1981.)  Using the same scheme they suggest, it is possible to conduct 
Monte Carlo tests of association with more complex structure than the 
simple permutation tests by (1) positing a baseline ERGM, (2) fitting it 
to your data, (3) simulating draws from the fitted model, and (4) 
examining the quantiles of the observed NLI/covariate interaction in the 
distribution of equivalent interactions generated by the simulated data. 
  Some properties of these tests are described in the above paper.  In 
practice, there are more ways for this to go wrong than the permutation 
test, and I would tend to favor the latter when feasible.  One case I 
_can_ think of in which the ERG-based test would be preferable would be 
when you want to test for an association of your covariate with a given 
NLI score, controlling for some other interaction of the same covariate 
with the target network (e.g., homophily).  A null of independence does 
not help you here, and a model-based test could prove efficacious.

4. Another, naive alternative would be to try to treat your problem in a 
standard regression framework, and try to patch things up in some 
fashion.  For some NLIs (e.g., degree) on large networks, we may suspect 
that there is relatively little dependence between observations, and the 
first-order properties of OLS are fairly robust in any case.  This is 
essentially the rationale behind network regression (where one typically 
pairs standard least squares estimators of parameters with multivariate 
QAP tests to assess significance), and it can work quite well.  Then 
again, the "patch and pray" approach can also fail, and you may or may 
not be able to tell when the answers you are getting partake heavily of 
fantasy.  I tend to encourage the use of more principled methods, where 
feasible.

That's my take on it, anyway.  My illustrious colleagues may or may not 
agree.

-Carter

PS. For the adventurous, an interesting technique might be to apply the 
permutation model (a la netperm) where the left-hand matrices consist 
entirely of diagonal matrices with individual NLI scores from the 
observed graph, and the right-hand matrices of consist entirely of 
diagonal matrices with individual covariate scores.  This would be a 
"vector" or "linear" version of the permutation model, analogous to the 
LAP versus QAP distinction in Hubert's terminology.  (It may be simpler 
to think of as a generalized location system model using only 
association terms based on node covariates as object features and NLI 
scores as location features, and with the support limited to 1:1 
assignments -- in fact, that's how I would implement it.  See the 
generalized location systems paper in Sociological Methodology (Butts, 
2007) for some idea of what I am prattling on about.)  I think it's safe 
to say that this application of that model family is not much 
explored...meaning that I'm not sure if anyone has tried it.  If someone 
has experimented with this application, I would be interesting in 
hearing about it.

On 7 September 2010 13:34, Carter T. Butts <buttsc@uci.edu> wrote:
> Hi, folks -
>
> Here is a four-part answer to this question:
>
> 1. If your goal is to test for marginal (non)association between an NLI
> (e.g., closeness) and a node-level covariate, IMHO the most straightforward
> approach is to use permutation procedures. ?If you want a quick tutorial,
> you might check out the associated portion of the statnet workshop we gave
> at this year's Political Networks meeting; the URL is
> http://lectopia.oit.duke.edu/ilectures/ilectures.lasso?ut=1065&id=27647, and
> the discussion starts at around 48 minutes. ?(Part 1 of the day's session is
> at http://lectopia.oit.duke.edu/ilectures/ilectures.lasso?ut=1065&id=27647,
> for those who are interested.) ? As I note in response to a question from
> the audience, generalizing this to the multivariate case is possible, but
> one runs into complications that make the approach less attractive. ?For the
> simple, bivariate case, however, my sense is that permutation tests are
> often a good starting point.
>
> 2. For more complex, parametric versions of the covariate/NLI question, the
> natural approach is to construct a statistic based on an interaction of the
> covariate with the NLI, and employ an ERG model. ?(This is equivalent to
> what nodecov does, with the NLI here being degree.) ?We have talked for
> years about adding equivalent terms for other centrality scores, but I am
> not sure if anything is implemented at present -- there are no special
> theoretical issues, but the computation can be painful. (I regularly hassle
> my CS colleagues for the algorithmic developments we need to make
> changescore calculation fast for indices like betweenness, but am assured
> that this is a non-trivial research problem. ?:-)) ?I spoke with Mark about
> putting something crude together a few months ago, but am not sure if he's
> had time to make progress on it -- it's clear that this would be a very
> interesting set of terms to be able to include. ?Having said that, we don't
> know how stable models built from those terms would be, so this might turn
> out to be harder in practice than it seems.
>
> 3. A fact little remembered today is that the ERG were introduced in part to
> act as non-trivial null models against which to test for complex structural
> biases. ?(See the discussion in Holland and Leinhardt, JASA, 1981.) ?Using
> the same scheme they suggest, it is possible to conduct Monte Carlo tests of
> association with more complex structure than the simple permutation tests by
> (1) positing a baseline ERGM, (2) fitting it to your data, (3) simulating
> draws from the fitted model, and (4) examining the quantiles of the observed
> NLI/covariate interaction in the distribution of equivalent interactions
> generated by the simulated data. ?Some properties of these tests are
> described in the above paper. ?In practice, there are more ways for this to
> go wrong than the permutation test, and I would tend to favor the latter
> when feasible. ?One case I _can_ think of in which the ERG-based test would
> be preferable would be when you want to test for an association of your
> covariate with a given NLI score, controlling for some other interaction of
> the same covariate with the target network (e.g., homophily). ?A null of
> independence does not help you here, and a model-based test could prove
> efficacious.
>
> 4. Another, naive alternative would be to try to treat your problem in a
> standard regression framework, and try to patch things up in some fashion.
> ?For some NLIs (e.g., degree) on large networks, we may suspect that there
> is relatively little dependence between observations, and the first-order
> properties of OLS are fairly robust in any case. ?This is essentially the
> rationale behind network regression (where one typically pairs standard
> least squares estimators of parameters with multivariate QAP tests to assess
> significance), and it can work quite well. ?Then again, the "patch and pray"
> approach can also fail, and you may or may not be able to tell when the
> answers you are getting partake heavily of fantasy. ?I tend to encourage the
> use of more principled methods, where feasible.
>
> That's my take on it, anyway. ?My illustrious colleagues may or may not
> agree.
>
> -Carter
>
> PS. For the adventurous, an interesting technique might be to apply the
> permutation model (a la netperm) where the left-hand matrices consist
> entirely of diagonal matrices with individual NLI scores from the observed
> graph, and the right-hand matrices of consist entirely of diagonal matrices
> with individual covariate scores. ?This would be a "vector" or "linear"
> version of the permutation model, analogous to the LAP versus QAP
> distinction in Hubert's terminology. ?(It may be simpler to think of as a
> generalized location system model using only association terms based on node
> covariates as object features and NLI scores as location features, and with
> the support limited to 1:1 assignments -- in fact, that's how I would
> implement it. ?See the generalized location systems paper in Sociological
> Methodology (Butts, 2007) for some idea of what I am prattling on about.) ?I
> think it's safe to say that this application of that model family is not
> much explored...meaning that I'm not sure if anyone has tried it. ?If
> someone has experimented with this application, I would be interesting in
> hearing about it.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Iasonas.  The issue (discovered by looking at the code you sent  
separately) is that when you read in a vector using the "read.table"  
command, it becomes an R object of type data.frame.  These objects can  
be a bit tricky to work with.

In your case, you had code like this:

Gender <-  read.table("Gender.csv",    <other stuff clipped out>)
mGender <- as.vector(Gender)
mGender[mGender=="1"]="Boy"
mGender[mGender=="2"]="Girl"
ng <-network(mat,directed=FALSE)
set.vertex.attribute(ng,"Gender",mGender)

The problem with this is that the "as.vector" function does not  
actually turn a data.frame object into a vector.  One way around this  
is to convert the data.frame into a matrix first, then a vector using
mGender <- as.vector(as.matrix(Gender))

But this is a bit clunky.  A slightly more efficient (if somewhat  
ugly) way is to simply grab the first column in the data.frame object,  
which can be done in a couple of different ways that are equivalent  
for data frames:

mGender <- Gender[[1]]
mGender <- Gender[,1]

In other words, your new code would look something like this:
Gender <-  read.table("Gender.csv",    <other stuff clipped out>)
mGender <- Gender[[1]]
mGender[mGender=="1"]="Boy"
mGender[mGender=="2"]="Girl"
ng <-network(mat,directed=FALSE)
set.vertex.attribute(ng,"Gender",mGender)

Of course, you'd do the same for all of your vertex attributes.

Hope this helps,
Dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bernadette.  You're mostly correct:  If one were to include  
"hamming distance from the observed network" as a statistic in an  
ERGM, then the minimum possible value of the statistic (zero) is  
achieved by the observed network.   According to well-established  
exponential family theory, whenever an observed statistic lies on the  
boundary of the convex hull of possible statistics, no maximum  
likelihood estimator exists.  Stated differently, in this case the MLE  
would essentially be negative infinity.

So _if_ one's goal is to obtain a maximum likelihood estimator of ergm  
parameters, then including "hamming distance from the observed  
network" is never a good idea.  However, there are other conceivable  
contexts (e.g., using descriptive statistics to classify networks)  
where it could make sense as a statistic.

I hope this helps.

Dave

>> right way of thinking? Would it make sense to include the hamming
>> distance to the observed network as a statistic in the model at all?
>> If so, when and when not?

Typically, one would not use the dependent network as "x" in an 
estimation context (although one might in a _simulation_ context, e.g. 
to generate perturbed data for robustness testing).  The "x" in the 
hamming term is usually some other network (e.g., the same system at an 
earlier time point, or another relation to which we believe that the 
modeled network may be related); its typical usage is thus closely 
analogous to edgecov.  As Dave noted, Hamming distance is also used in 
other contexts as a tool for graph comparison (see, e.g., hdist in sna), 
but that's a somewhat different matter.

Hope that helps,

-Carter
